fields.title: Skoba: Small Business Churn Is Rising, with Four Theories
fields.summary: Price, competitor, support, or redesign. Decide how to get clarity within a quarter.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do this quarter?
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager responsible for retention in the self-serve part of the product.
fields.brief/company: Skoba is a fictional 200-person company selling customer support software.
fields.brief/context: Monthly churn in the SMB segment (up to 20 seats, self-serve, 41% of revenue) grew from 3.1% to 3.9% over two quarters. Enterprise churn remains stable at 0.7%. Leadership asks for a plan. Four theories are circulating: a price increase eight months ago, a competitor with a free tier, degraded support response time, and a redesigned inbox screen released five months ago that some users disliked.
fields.brief/objective: Understand the root cause and structure the quarter to get a definitive answer.
fields.brief/constraints: One quarter, four developers. Analytics can build cohorts in a week. Mass surveying churned users is not possible: it requires explicit opt-in consent, and response rates are historically under 3%.
fields.brief/task: Choose your course of action and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Four theories are a day's work, not a quarter's
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Most hypotheses can be eliminated through segment breakdowns: if a metric worsened equally for both affected and unaffected users, that change isn't the cause. The remainder usually boils down to two events that coincided in time, which cannot be separated using historical data alone—you need a control group. That control group converts a quarter of guesswork into six weeks of verifiable answers.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Redesigned inbox screen was released five months ago to all users.

Weekly activity per account in SMB, before and after:
— 1–4 seats: 3.1 → 2.4 sessions per week;
— 5–19 seats: 6.8 → 6.9 sessions per week.

The redesign introduced a triage side panel built for multiple operators. On 1–4 seat accounts, it takes up about 30% of the screen, and analytics shows users interact with it in only 4% of their sessions.

CSAT score in SMB dropped by 11 points after the redesign, while enterprise remained unchanged.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Monthly churn for 1–4 seat accounts over nine months:
3.5 — 3.6 — 3.5 — 3.7 — 3.6 — 3.8 — 4.4 — 4.7 — 4.9.

Price increase: end of month 3. Competitor free tier: month 5. Inbox redesign: also month 5.

Note from analytics alongside the table: "The redesign and the competitor launch hit the exact same month. We cannot separate them using historical data."

Support: average first response time increased from 4.2 to 5.1 hours over the same two quarters.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Adapt the inbox for small accounts and test via experiment
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Collapse the side panel by default for accounts under 5 seats, roll it out to half of them, and use the control group to isolate the redesign effect from the competitor.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Segment breakdowns point to a single segment: 1–4 seats drive the churn increase from 3.5% to 4.9%, while 5–19 seats remain flat. Pricing cohorts shifted equally, meaning price does not explain the difference.
Timing also aligns: activity on small accounts dropped from 3.1 to 2.4 sessions per week after the redesign, while larger ones stayed unchanged.
The redesign and competitor launched in the same month, making historical isolation impossible—however, an experiment can separate them. Half of small accounts get the collapsed panel, half don't: this is the only way to get a proven answer rather than another opinion.
After six weeks, activity in the collapsed panel group recovers to 3.0 sessions, with churn at 3.9% vs. 4.8% in control.
The rest of the quarter is spent fully adapting the screen for small-account workflows.
Trade-off: the competitor hasn't gone anywhere, and part of the team feels you focused on a secondary issue.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Spend the first six weeks recruiting and interviewing churned 1–4 seat accounts, then decide how to spend the rest of the quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Recruitment is difficult, as expected: response rate is under 3%, yielding only nine interviews over six weeks.
The interviews offer useful insights: five mention it "became inconvenient," three cite the competitor, two mention price.
This aligns with segment breakdowns, but still fails to separate the redesign from the competitor—they happened in the same month, and users confound them in conversations.
By week six, you know roughly what cohort data already showed, with half the quarter remaining.
Trade-off: a qualitative method was applied to a question that required a control group; however, one insight emerged solely from calls—users didn't know the panel could be collapsed manually.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Counter the competitor with a low-cost tier
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Assume the free tier is the cause and launch a low-cost or free plan for accounts under 5 seats within the quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The plan launches in two months and slows churn among the smallest users: 1–4 seat churn drops from 4.9% to 4.3%.
However, SMB revenue falls even faster: some 5–19 seat accounts split up to qualify for the new plan.
Meanwhile, "too expensive" was checked by 24 out of 61 respondents at a 2.8% response rate—that's 24 people out of thousands who churned, and pricing cohorts shifted identically.
The redesigned screen remains inconvenient for those accounts, and activity stays flat at 2.4 sessions per week.
Trade-off: the loudest hypothesis was assumed to be the cause, and the response was subsidized at the expense of revenue, despite breakdown data showing price wasn't the driver.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: First response time increased from 4.2 to 5.1 hours. Hire support staff to restore it.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Hiring and training take the quarter, bringing response time back to 4.3 hours.
Churn on 1–4 seat accounts stays at 4.8%: for enterprise clients, who write to support significantly more often, churn didn't change at all over both quarters.
This hypothesis was validated neither by breakdowns nor experiments—it was chosen simply because the metric degraded over the same timeframe.
The inbox redesign was left untouched, the competitor went unstudied, and the quarter ended.
Trade-off: a temporal coincidence was mistaken for causation, despite the most severely impacted segment contacting support less frequently than others.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Considering the first idea mentioned instead of evaluating multiple options
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Idea selection is determined by who proposed it
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Evaluating a solution as a monolithic block instead of testing its independent parameters
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A hypothesis lacking magnitude or mechanism—it cannot be disproved
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Ideas are compared solely on expected upside, ignoring the cost of inaction
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Next steps for each potential outcome were not defined in advance
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Sample size and timeline were not calculated before launch, monitoring results ad-hoc
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: An expensive test was chosen where a prototype or feature flag toggle would have sufficed
